text: Aert van der Neer painted moonlit scenes and snowy winter landscapes, often looking down a canal or river. Houbraken says he worked as a steward to the lords of Arkel, which would explain why no early pictures survive. His landscapes sold poorly, so he opened a wine tavern in 1659, and he went broke two years later. He died in poverty, and the pictures he left were valued at about five shillings apiece. His son Eglon became a portrait painter. Van der Neer died in 1677.

Eugen Jettel moved to Paris in 1873 for a well-paid job with the Austrian art dealer Charles Sedelmeyer, who may have hoped he would marry his daughter. Jettel married a Viennese glovemaker's daughter instead. Sedelmeyer cut his salary, and the couple fell into financial distress. He still became the centre of a circle of Austrian and German artists in Paris, with ties to the Barbizon school. An inheritance let him return to Vienna in 1897, where he was a founding member of the Vienna Secession.

Godfried Schalcken studied with Samuel van Hoogstraten in Dordrecht and then moved to Leiden, to the studio of Gerard Dou, and his early genre pictures look very like Dou's. Like Dou, he specialised in small scenes lit by candlelight. He spent five years in England, but his rough manners and bad temper put society off. Houbraken, his pupil, singled out Lady, Come into the Garden at Buckingham Palace as typical of his work. Schalcken settled in The Hague and died there in 1706.

John Thomas Serres learned to paint from his father Dominic, a founder of the Royal Academy. After his father's death he became Marine Painter to the King, and he also taught drawing at the Royal Naval College in Chelsea. His career suffered when his wife Olivia insisted she was the illegitimate daughter of a royal duke and demanded to be called Princess Olive of Cumberland. Serres tried to win back his losses by setting up the Royal Coburg Theatre, later the Old Vic, but she ruined him again. He died in a London debtors' prison in 1825.

Jan Gossart was the name he used in his lifetime, and the Dutch spelling Gossaert crept in later, even though French was his first language. He is also called Jan Mabuse, after Maubeuge. He was among the first painters from the Low Countries to visit Italy and Rome, in 1508 and 1509, and he brought home Italian ideas in the style called Romanism. His patrons were mostly in the Habsburg family circle, among them Philip of Burgundy and the exiled Christian II of Denmark. He was no printmaker, so his fame spread less widely than Dürer's.

Jean Augustin Daiwaille came from Cologne and studied in Amsterdam under Adriaan de Lelie. He later settled in Rotterdam, where he did well painting portraits. In the 1820s he was an early champion of lithography, overseeing the installation of a press at the new Royal Academy and teaching students the technique. He then started his own lithographic business, which printed reproductions of his paintings and copies of work by others, such as Barend Cornelis Koekkoek. Koekkoek married his daughter Elise Thérèse. Daiwaille died in 1850.

Lesser Ury's first exhibition in 1889 got a hostile reception, though Adolph Menzel championed him. He came from a baker's family in Birnbaum in Prussia, and he studied painting at the Düsseldorf academy. He painted nocturnal cafe scenes and rainy streets, and he quickly repeated those compositions to sell them while keeping the originals. The copies hurt his reputation. Later he showed with the Berlin Secession, and in 1922 he had a major exhibition. Introverted and distrustful, he grew reclusive and died in Berlin in 1931.

Philipp Kilian engraved a portrait of Joachim von Sandrart and illustrated Sandrart's Teutsche Academie. The RKD says he was the son of the engraver Wolfgang Kilian and the brother of Bartholomäus. He also made engravings after paintings by Karel Skreta, Philippe de Champaigne and Johann Carl Loth. He worked in the German Baroque style, and he lived from 1628 to 1693.

Nicolas Béatrizet signed his plates N. B. L. F., and there are a great many of them. He came from Lunéville and worked in Rome, where he engraved for about twenty years, partly under Michelangelo's direction. His style suggests he trained with Giorgio Ghisi and Agostino Veneziano, though that is a guess. Joseph Strutt thought the value of his prints lay in being unique records of pictures by some of the greatest artists, not in the quality of the engraving. He died in Rome after 1560.

Célestin Nanteuil's elder brother Charles-François was a noted sculptor who won the Prix de Rome in 1817. Célestin himself was born in Rome to French parents who belonged to Joseph Bonaparte's entourage. He entered the École des Beaux-Arts and studied under Eustache-Hyacinthe Langlois, then worked in the studio of Ingres. He later became director of the Académie des beaux-arts and curator of the Musée des beaux-arts in Dijon. He died in Bourron-Marlotte at 60.

Nobody is sure whether Louis Bernard Coclers was born in Liège or Maastricht in 1740. His father Jean-Baptiste taught him, and he spent three years in Italy before settling in Maastricht. He moved on to Nijmegen and Dordrecht, and from 1769 to Leiden. Politically compromised, he left Holland in 1787 for Paris and stayed several years. Back in Amsterdam he painted portraits and engraved cabinet pictures in the manner of Frans van Mieris the Elder and Gabriël Metsu. He engraved 166 plates, signed with a cipher or his initials.

Thomas Chippendale published a book of furniture designs in 1754, The Gentleman and Cabinet Maker's Director, which created a mass market for furniture. He came from Otley in Yorkshire, the only child of a joiner. He probably learned the basics from his father, and he's believed to have trained with Richard Wood in York before moving to London. The Victoria and Albert Museum says his designs were so influential that Chippendale became shorthand for any furniture like them. A padouk cabinet of his sold at auction in 2008 for £2,729,250. He was buried in 1779.

Pierre-Antoine Demachy painted ruins, trompe-l'oeil architecture and imagined scenes of Paris. He was the son of a carpenter and became a student of the stage designer Giovanni Niccolò Servandoni. Soon after, the Académie royale certified him as a Painter of Architecture, and he showed at the Salon from 1757 until 1802. His trompe-l'oeil paintings for the front of the new Church of Sainte-Geneviève, now the Panthéon, earned him the job of decorating stage sets for the Menus-Plaisirs du Roi. He died in 1807.

James Gabriel Huquier, originally Jacques-Gabriel, helped his father Gabriel with many of his engravings. The father worked in the style of Watteau and Boucher, and his designs for furniture, silver and other ornament helped set styles under Louis XV. In 1758 the son married the daughter of the engraver Jacques Chéreau and worked with his father-in-law as an engraver and printseller. They opened a shop for wallpapers and prints in 1764 and a wallpaper factory two years later. One of his portrait subjects was the Chevalier d'Eon.

According to the RKD, Richard Collin was a pupil of Joachim von Sandrart in Rome and became a master in the Antwerp Guild of St. Luke around 1650. He worked in Rome and Antwerp and is known for portraits he engraved for Cornelis de Bie's book of artists, Het Gulden Cabinet. Later he took on pupils. In 1678 he moved to Brussels as court engraver to Charles II of Spain. His engraving of Queen Christina of Sweden is in the Victoria and Albert Museum. Collin was born in Luxembourg and died in Brussels in 1698.

Pietro da Cortona took the name of his native town, and he was born Pietro Berrettini. He worked mainly in Rome and Florence and is best known for his frescoed ceilings, such as the vault of the main salon of the Palazzo Barberini in Rome. He painted large schemes for the Medici family in Florence and for the Oratorian fathers at Santa Maria in Vallicella. He also designed buildings, though few of them were built. Bernini and Borromini were his contemporaries and rivals. He died in 1669.

Over 30 of Meindert Hobbema's paintings show water mills. He was a pupil of Jacob van Ruisdael and specialised in sunny forest scenes with roads and glistening ponds, and in flat landscapes with scattered groups of trees. His best-known painting, The Avenue at Middelharnis, is a different sort of scene. Most of his mature works come from the 1660s. When he married and took a job as an exciseman he painted less, and from 1689 apparently not at all. He died in 1709.

Józef Pankiewicz went to Paris in 1889 with his studio partner Władysław Podkowiński for the Exposition Universelle, and he won a silver medal there for a painting of a vegetable market. He had studied at the School of Fine Arts in Warsaw under Wojciech Gerson and Aleksander Kamiński. After winning a scholarship he went to the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg. Pankiewicz was a Polish impressionist painter, graphic artist and teacher. He spent much of his career in France and died in 1940.

James Seymour painted horses, and he also owned and raced them. His father was an art dealer who also worked as a banker, goldsmith and diamond merchant, and that income left the boy free to teach himself art. Sir William Jolliffe and Charles Seymour, the 6th Duke of Somerset, were among his patrons. Horse racing ended up ruining him financially. Along with John Wootton and Peter Tillemans he is counted as one of the three founders of the sporting school of painting. He died in 1752.

Wouter Johannes van Troostwijk never became a full-time artist. After 1805 he worked as concierge at Amsterdam City Hall, where he lived and had his studio, and he painted before and after work. His father, a cloth merchant better known as a chemist and physicist, had scientists as guests at home, which inspired his interest in nature. He used his days off to paint outdoors. One cold autumn night he worked too long, caught a high fever and died a few days later, in 1810. Only eight of his paintings are on public display.

Albert Lebourg taught drawing in Algiers after the Rouen art collector Laurent Laperlier noticed him, and he stayed there until 1877. He came back to Paris with many paintings of the casbah and the mosques. In 1879 he showed 30 of them at the Fourth Impressionist Exhibition, next to work by Monet. A year later he showed 20 works of Rouen, Paris and Algiers. He belongs to the Rouen School and painted more than 2,000 landscapes. He died in Rouen in 1928.

Friedrich Gauermann's father wanted him to be a farmer, but an elder brother who died young pushed him toward art. He studied landscape under his father and copied the animal painters he found in the Vienna academy and court library. Two animal pictures shown in Vienna in 1824 brought commissions from Prince Metternich and the French ambassador Caraman. His picture The Storm, exhibited in 1829, raised his reputation, and his works sold at high prices after that. He often showed the free life of animals in wild mountain scenery. He died in Vienna in 1862.

Tamamura Kōzaburō opened a photographic studio in Asakusa, Tokyo, in 1874, and in 1883 he moved to Yokohama. The Yokohama studio, which he opened after nine years in Asakusa, became his most successful one. He was one of the originators of the Yokohama shashin photographic scene. His studio was still operating in 1909. The collection here includes his book The Silk Industry of Japan.

His uncle David Klöcker Ehrenstrahl, court painter in Sweden, called David Krafft over from Hamburg in 1675 to be his assistant and apprentice. Krafft had been orphaned early. The Queen paid him a yearly grant for a journey to Italy by way of the princely courts, where he was to paint her relatives. He spent a year in Venice, three years in Rome and one in Bologna, then went on to Vienna and Paris. When Ehrenstrahl died in 1698, Krafft succeeded him as painter to the Swedish Royal Court. He died in 1724.

Charles Bird King was four when his father was killed by Native Americans near Marietta, Ohio. His mother took him back to her parents' home in Newport. At fifteen he went to New York to study under Edward Savage, and at twenty he moved to London to study with Benjamin West at the Royal Academy. The War of 1812 sent him home after seven years, and he settled in Washington, DC. His portraits of Native American leaders are his best known work, though his depictions of the culture have been called inaccurate. He died in 1862.

Armand Rassenfosse was expected to run his family's shop in Liège, which sold home furnishings and decorative art, but an uncle gave him a few etchings by Félicien Rops and he became intrigued with etching. By 1882, unknown to his family, he was sending drawings signed Zig to the satirical journal Le Frondeur. In 1884 he showed his work to Adrien de Witte, who encouraged him to try new techniques, including pyrography. He was largely self-taught. His set of illustrations for Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du mal is called his masterwork. He died in 1934.

Jan Miense Molenaer shared a studio with his wife, Judith Leyster, who was also a genre painter. Both of them may have been pupils of Frans Hals. Early in his career Molenaer worked in a style close to Hals, and later his style came closer to Adriaen van Ostade's. His genre scenes often showed people playing music, as well as taverns and card games. He also set biblical stories in his own time, such as The Denying of Peter in a Dutch tavern. Molenaer was born and died in Haarlem.

When the Spanish army besieged Haarlem in 1573, the parents of Cornelis van Haarlem fled, but he stayed behind and was raised by the painter Pieter Pietersz the Elder, his first teacher. He later studied in Rouen and in Antwerp with Gillis Coignet before returning to Haarlem for good. He belonged to the Haarlem Mannerists, who took their cue from drawings by Bartholomeus Spranger. His early works were large and highly stylised, with Italianate nudes in twisted poses and unnatural anatomy. Later his style turned to the Netherlandish realist tradition. He died in 1638.

Sebastian Furck lived in Rome early in his life and was already engraving plates there in 1612. He later spent ten years in Frankfurt am Main, where he engraved many portraits and historical pieces, mostly for booksellers. They include plates of the Colonna family and some after Titian. He worked mainly with the graver, though a few etchings by him exist. When he did not sign a plate with his name, he marked it with a cipher. He died at Frankfurt in 1666.

Cornelis Bos took his surname from 's Hertogenbosch, where he is registered until the late 1530s. By 1541 he was in Antwerp, where he became a citizen and joined the Guild of St. Luke. He is known for accurate engravings of Italian works, and he often signed with the monogram C-B. In Antwerp his engravings illustrated Dutch editions of Vitruvius and Serlio, published by Pieter Coecke van Aelst. In the summer of 1544 he was forced to flee the city. He died before 7 May 1555.

John Rubens Smith studied art first with his father, the mezzotint engraver John Raphael Smith, and later at the Royal Academy. Around 1807 he left London for New York City. He showed the United States in the decades before photography, and his drawing academies and drawing manuals influenced a generation of American artists. His son John Rowson Smith was a moving panorama painter. Smith died in New York in 1849.

Pieter Codde is said to have studied with Frans Hals, but he more likely trained with Barent van Someren, a portrait painter, innkeeper, actor and art dealer. In 1625, at a party on Van Someren's estate, Codde got into a fight with his friend Cornelis Duyster that ended in bloodshed when they hit each other in the face with jars. His earliest known work is a Portrait of a Young Man from 1626. By 1628 he was living in a fashionable Amsterdam street full of painters. When he died, his maid inherited most of his property.

Nicolaas van der Waay designed stamps, coins and banknotes, and he made the allegorical illustrations for the Golden Coach. His first drawing lessons came from Louis Koopman, whose daughter he later married. He studied at the Rijksacademie from 1871 to 1875, and later he taught there for many years, first as a lecturer and then as a professor. A series of his paintings shows the lives of the girls at the Amsterdam Orphanage. His work was also part of the painting event in the art competition at the 1928 Summer Olympics.

Willem Maris said he worked outdoors from the time he was young, sitting in the meadow to watch the cows before and after school. Writers often call him self-taught, though his brothers Jacob and Matthijs, both painters, gave him part of his training. His debut came in 1862 with Cows on the Heath, and that year he first visited Oosterbeek. There he met Gerard Bilders and Anton Mauve, and he stayed friends with Mauve for the rest of their lives. He was a Hague School landscape painter and died in 1910.

Henry William Cave left Oxford at eighteen and went to Ceylon as private secretary to the Anglican Bishop of Colombo. There he edited the diocesan magazine and grew interested in printing and photography. With the bishop's encouragement he opened a bookstore in Colombo in 1876, mainly selling bibles and religious tracts. By 1884 his firm, H. W. Cave and Company, was a well established printing and publishing business that also sold musical instruments and sporting goods, such as billiard tables, rickshaws and bicycles. He died in 1913.

Charles-Joseph Natoire is remembered above all for the History of Psyche, painted for an oval salon in the Hôtel de Soubise in Paris, and for the designs of the History of Don Quixote series, woven at Beauvais. His father, a sculptor, taught him drawing, then sent him to Paris to study with Louis Galloche and François Lemoyne. He won the Prix de Rome in 1721. From 1751 he directed the French Academy in Rome for more than twenty years. In his own lifetime he was considered the equal of François Boucher. He died in 1777.

For about five years Jan Gillisz. van Vliet turned Rembrandt's designs into etchings. One account says he was Rembrandt's collaborator, not his pupil, and that Rembrandt began his own etching career with him and soon outstripped him. Their work together ended when Van Vliet married a rich woman and turned to managing her estate. He made no prints after that. He is remembered for his drawings and prints, including a popular series of beggars. His paintings are no longer attributed to him with any certainty, and he lived in Leiden from 1605 to 1668.

Jean-Baptiste Marie Pierre studied under Charles-Joseph Natoire at the Académie royale and painted a self-portrait in 1732. He was Premier peintre du Roi from 1770 until 1789. Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun wrote in her memoirs that Pierre, then First Painter to the King, strongly opposed her admission to the Académie because he did not want women admitted. She called him a very mediocre painter. His own students included Étienne-Louis Boullée, Louis-Jacques Durameau and Antoine Vestier.

Jean de Paleologu often signed his work Pal or PAL. Born in Bucharest, he trained in England, attended a military academy in Romania and then moved to Paris, before leaving for the United States in 1900. He illustrated Catulle Mendès's Petits poèmes russes and drew for periodicals such as Vanity Fair, Strand Magazine and Rire. Portraits of comedians and music-hall performers were another subject. He made poster advertisements for bicycle makers such as Déesse. Late in life he worked in applied graphics and died in Miami Beach in 1942.

Jan Cornelisz. Vermeyen, also known as Juan del Mayo, went along with Emperor Charles V on his military campaign to Tunis in 1535. He worked mainly in Mechelen as a portraitist for the Habsburg governors Archduchess Margaret of Austria and Mary of Hungary. Margaret made him her court painter and paid him an annual stipend of 100 Flemish pounds. It is not clear with whom he trained, but his early work resembles that of Jan van Scorel and Jan Gossaert. His will of 1559 was rediscovered only in 1998. In it he gave his age as 55.

H. Siddons Mowbray lost both parents young. His father died a year after he was born, and his mother was burnt in a domestic accident when he was five. His aunt and her husband, George Mowbray, adopted him. After a year at West Point he went to Paris and entered the atelier of Léon Bonnat in 1879, and his first picture, Aladdin, brought him public notice. He was best known for decorative work, such as a ceiling for the Vanderbilt mansion in Hyde Park. He directed the American Academy in Rome from 1902 and died in 1928.

Egbert van Panderen worked in Antwerp for about ten years and then in Amsterdam. He joined the Antwerp Guild of St. Luke in 1606. Mostly he made reproductive prints, among them engravings after Rubens. His style can be recognised by hard lines with strong contrast. He was probably born in Haarlem, though the Dutch Wikipedia puts a question mark on that, and he died in 1637.

Jean Moyreau engraved mostly the works of Antoine Watteau and Philips Wouwerman, for the Recueil Crozat and the collection of Jean de Jullienne. He came to Paris from Orléans, studied with Bon Boullogne and became a member of the Académie royale. He showed at the Salon from 1737 to 1761. His portrait of the violinist Jean-Féry Rebel after Watteau is among his prints. Moyreau had his shop on the rue Galande in Paris and died there in 1762.

Lucas van Valckenborch left Antwerp with his brother Marten in 1566, probably for religious reasons, as they may have been Protestants. A painted view of Liège and other topographical views show that he travelled up the Meuse, a trip that taught him to work straight from nature. In Aachen he met his brother again, and their friend Hans Vredeman de Vries joined them for two years. Archduke Matthias hired him as court painter, impressed above all by his portraits. Valckenborch died in Frankfurt in 1597.

Pierre Petit learned photography in Paris in the workshop of André-Adolphe-Eugène Disdéri, together with 76 other employees. In 1858 he opened his own workshop with Antoine René Trinquart, and it did so well that branches followed in Baden-Baden and Marseille. He was the official photographer of the International Exposition of 1867. He went to New York several times to report on the building of the Statue of Liberty and made many photographs of the Siege of Paris. Late in life he tried underwater photography. He died in 1909.

François de Cuvilliés first came to the notice of the exiled Elector Max Emanuel of Bavaria as a court dwarf. The Elector saw his aptitude, had him tutored in mathematics and sent him to Paris to train in the atelier of Jean-François Blondel. Back in Munich he became court architect. His fame was established by the decor of the Reiche Zimmer in the Munich Residenz, after a fire damaged it in 1729. He also designed the hunting lodge Falkenlust at Schloss Brühl and the Amalienburg in the Nymphenburg park. He died in Munich in 1768.

Louis Surugue is still often confused with his son Pierre-Louis, who signed his work P. L. Surugue. Louis studied with Bernard Picart and went with him to the Netherlands in 1710. After he came back to France in 1715, he set up on the rue des Noyers in Paris as a maker and seller of prints. By partnering with the picture dealer Edme-François Gersaint he got a monopoly on engraved copies of Charles Antoine Coypel and Antoine Watteau. In 1721 he also won an exclusive licence to print and sell engravings after Coypel's drawings.

Joannes van Doetecum the Elder is known for etchings after genre scenes by Pieter Bruegel the Elder and for maps of Dutch cities. Like his father Jan, he worked as a glazier when he was young, and his brother Bartholt kept the family business going. He moved from Deventer to Haarlem in 1578. With his brother Lucas he made many print series. Three of his sons also worked as artists, among them Baptista, who was a cartographer, engraver and publisher. He died in Haarlem in 1605.

Gustave Van de Woestijne belonged to the First Group of Latem, artists who worked in the rural village of Sint-Martens-Latem on the Lys, near Ghent. His brother Karel was a Flemish poet. The Royal Museum of Fine Arts in Antwerp holds his The Blind Man, The Sleepers, The Liqueur Drinkers and Azure, among other works. He painted as a Belgian expressionist. He was made a Knight of the Order of Leopold in 1919, and he is buried in the Campo Santo cemetery.

The Imprimerie nationale began as the Royal Imprimery, founded by Louis XIII in 1640 at the urging of Cardinal Richelieu. It followed the printers to the king that Francis I had named earlier. Its name changed with the regime, from Imprimery of the Republic after the Revolution to Imperial under Napoleon, until the Third Republic settled on the current name in 1870. Today it is a government-owned French company that produces secure documents such as identity cards and passports. It was partially privatized in 1993, though the state still holds all of its shares.

Nobody is sure where Gillis Neyts was born. Probably it was Ghent, where he was baptized in 1623, but a record from Namur calls him a native of Overijse and one album of drawings says Lille. It is not clear whom he trained with. Lucas van Uden has been named, though there is no evidence. He married Clara de la Porte in Antwerp and joined the guild there as a master painter and engraver in 1647. Today he is known mainly for Italianising and topographical drawings of the Southern Netherlands, and he died in 1678.

Jan Miel was probably born in Beveren-Waas, though Antwerp and 's-Hertogenbosch have also been suggested. Nobody knows who trained him. The Italian biographer Passeri names Anthony van Dyck, but there is no independent evidence. He is documented in Rome from 1636 to 1658, where he joined the Bentvueghels. At first he belonged to the Bamboccianti, who painted scenes of the Roman lower classes, but later he moved to history subjects in a classicising style. He ended his career in Turin as court painter to Charles Emanuel II, Duke of Savoy.

Gaspar de Crayer was the son of an Antwerp decorative painter, illuminator and art dealer, but he looked for opportunity in Brussels. He is believed to have studied under Raphael Coxie, court painter to the governors of the Spanish Netherlands. He became a master in the Brussels guild in 1607 and served as its dean for several years. He painted many Counter-Reformation altarpieces and portraits, including portraits of the kings of Spain. As court painter to the governors he helped spread the Rubens style across Flanders. He stayed in Brussels until 1664 and died in 1669.

Konrad Krzyżanowski was expelled from the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg after his distaste for its teaching methods grew into a conflict with the Rector. He grew up in Kyiv, where Mykola Murashko gave him his first art lessons. In 1897 he moved to Munich for private lessons with Simon Hollósy, and three years later he settled in Warsaw. There he and Kazimierz Stabrowski ran a painting school for four years. From 1904 he taught at the Academy of Fine Arts, often taking his students to paint outdoors in Lithuania and Finland. He died in 1922.

Pieter Saenredam painted whitewashed church interiors, working from precise measurements of the building and careful sketches made on site. He was the son of the printmaker Jan Pietersz Saenredam and was born in Assendelft. In 1612 he moved permanently to Haarlem, where he became a pupil of Frans de Grebber. In 1623 he joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke. A drawing in the British Museum by his friend Jacob van Campen shows him as very short and hunchbacked. He was buried in Haarlem in 1665.

Francesco Villamena moved to Rome around 1590 and studied under Cornelis Cort. He took in parts of Agostino Carracci's graphic approach and drew inspiration from northern Mannerist engravers such as Hendrick Goltzius and Jacques Bellange. He engraved mostly religious and historical subjects. A series on the life of Saint Francis followed his first original engraving, a Last Judgement. In 1599 the calligrapher Ludovico Curione commissioned a series of plates with typefaces and decorative frames. Villamena also taught drawing and collected art, and he died in 1624.

Ernest Lawson showed with the American group The Eight, who formed a loose association in 1908 to protest the narrow taste and restrictive exhibition policies of the National Academy of Design. He was born in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and arrived in the United States as a teenager. He studied at the Art Students League under John Twachtman, who introduced him to Impressionism. Lawson was mainly a landscape painter, with a small number of realistic urban scenes. His style falls between Impressionism and realism. He died in 1939.

Johann Friedrich August Tischbein is called the Leipziger Tischbein, one of a large family of artists. His father, a set painter, gave him his first lessons, and at eighteen he went to Kassel to work in the studios of his uncle Johann Heinrich Tischbein. He studied with Johann Georg Wille in Paris, and in Rome he worked with Jacques-Louis David. Back in Germany he became court painter to the Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont, who sent him to the Netherlands three times to improve his portraits. Later he went to Berlin as an independent portrait painter. He died in 1812.

Friedrich Friedländer studied at the Vienna Academy and then under Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller, and he visited Italy, Düsseldorf and finally Paris. He began with historical pictures and caused a sensation with The Death of Tasso. After 1854 he painted genre pictures exclusively, with subjects from military life and the local life of Vienna. His scenes from Swabian folk life are well known. He later became Friedrich Ritter von Friedländer-Malheim and died in Vienna in 1901.

Johan Gustaf Sandberg was foremost a history painter who used settings from Norse mythology and Swedish history. His frescoes in Uppsala Cathedral, which show King Gustav Vasa, are his most widely known work. He became a student at the preparatory school of the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts in 1794. He also studied music and learned to play keyboard instruments, and he earned money by giving music lessons and working in the Academy's decoration workshop. Besides history paintings he made a number of portraits. He died in 1854.

Gustaf Nordenskiöld was the first to study the ancient Pueblo cliff dwellings in Mesa Verde scientifically. He was the eldest son of the polar explorer Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld. After graduating from Uppsala he travelled to Svalbard and brought a collection of plant fossils back to the Swedish Museum of Natural History. Then he was diagnosed with tuberculosis and went to Berlin for treatment. His photographs of Mesa Verde date from 1891. He died in 1895.

Simon François Ravenet studied engraving in Paris under Jacques-Philippe Le Bas, moved to London in 1750 and founded a school of line engraving there, and he is credited with reviving engraving in England. His pupils included John Hall and William Wynne Ryland. He was one of William Hogarth's assistants. Mostly he put other artists' works into engraved form. He developed Décalquer, the technique that gave decal its name. He died in London in 1774.

Giuseppe Canella started out making stage sets and decorating stately homes in Verona and Mantua, after training with his father Giovanni, who worked as an architect. He may have taken up landscape painting under the influence of Pietro Ronzoni, and his first views came only after a short stay in Venice in 1815. A long journey through Spain, the Netherlands and France followed. Thirteen landscapes shown at the Brera in 1831 were a great success with the public and critics. Later he turned to urban views. He died in 1847.

Orazio Borgianni was taught to paint by his brother Giulio, called Scalzo. Spanish patronage drew him to Spain, where he signed an inventory in 1605 and a petition to start an Italianate academy of painting. For the Convento de Portacoeli in Valladolid he made a series of nine paintings, which are still there. The Prado holds two of his pictures from that time, a St Christopher and a Stigmatization of St Francis. Back in Rome he worked for the Spanish ambassador and for churches, and he painted frescoes in the apse of San Silvestro in Capite. He died in 1616.

Giulio Pippi, known as Giulio Romano, began his career in Rome as a young assistant to Raphael. He worked on the frescoes of the Raphael Rooms and the Vatican loggias from Raphael's designs, and he helped decorate the ceiling of the Villa Farnesina. After Raphael died in 1520, he took a leading role in finishing the Vatican commissions, among them the frescoes of the life of Constantine. He also decorated the Villa Madama for Cardinal Giuliano de' Medici, later Clement VII. Marcantonio Raimondi engraved prints of his drawings, which helped spread the style across Europe. He died in 1546.

Thomas Sidney Cooper's father deserted the family when the boy was five, and there was no money for tuition, or even for paper and pencils. By twelve he was working as a coach painter, and later as a scenery painter with a travelling theatre company. At twenty he went to London, drew in the British Museum and was admitted as a student of the Royal Academy. He could not afford to stay, so he went back to Canterbury and worked as a drawing master. He is noted for small groups of cows or sheep at rest. He died in 1902.

Dissatisfied with his own work, Eugen Bracht moved to Berlin in 1864 and became a merchant. In 1876 he came back to painting and joined his former teacher Karl Ludwig Seeger in Karlsruhe. He was known for moody landscapes and coastal scenes in North Germany, and he made a sketching trip through Syria, Palestine and Egypt. He painted the Battle of Chattanooga for a cyclorama that was installed in Philadelphia and Kansas City. Later he became a representative of German Impressionism. He taught at the Dresden Academy and died in 1921.

Giuseppe Maria Crespi got the nickname Lo Spagnuolo, the Spaniard, because he wore tight clothes in the Spanish fashion of his day. At about twelve he apprenticed with Angelo Michele Toni, and from fifteen to eighteen he worked under Domenico Maria Canuti. Carlo Maratti is said to have invited him to Rome, but he declined. In 1681 Carlo Cignani invited him to join an Accademia del Nudo, and he stayed in that studio until 1686. After that he worked independently. He painted religious pictures and portraits, but he is best known for genre scenes.

Jules-Alexandre Grün worked at a large printing company in Paris, where his artistic director was Jules Chéret, who was also his main competitor in poster art. He made posters and illustrations. Several of his posters were published in Les Maîtres de l'Affiche. His best known painting is The Dinner Party, from 1911. A French Post-Impressionist painter, poster artist and illustrator, he died in 1938.

Jan Stolker worked as a printmaker, painter, painting dealer and art collector. He was born in Amsterdam on 1 July 1724 and became a pupil of Jan Maurits Quinkhard. He is known for portraits and for copies of 17th-century artists, and he was a member of the Confrerie Pictura and of the Rotterdam Guild of Saint Luke. Stolker died in Rotterdam. The date was 10 June 1785.

Carl Wilhelm Kolbe was called the Elder to tell him apart from his nephew, a painter of the same name. His father made wallpaper and did goldwork. Kolbe taught French at the Philanthropinum in Dessau, and under the influence of a distant relative, Daniel Chodowiecki, he took up painting and drawing. When the school closed he chose a career in art and studied in Berlin with Chodowiecki and Asmus Carstens. His first etching portfolios, mostly of landscapes, appeared in these years. In 1798 he became court copper engraver in Dessau, and he died there in 1835.

Anna Boberg came from an artistic family but never had formal training in the arts, and she is considered self-taught. She began with ceramics and textiles, creating the Peacock vase for Rörstrand, and she also worked in set design and writing. After a trip to northern Norway in 1901 she painted there for many years, often near Lofoten, where she eventually had a cabin. Sweden received these works badly, but Paris did much better. She met her husband, the architect Ferdinand Boberg, in Paris, and they were engaged in 1884.

Joshua Cristall was for a time president of the Society of Painters in Water-Colours. His father, a Scot, bitterly opposed his artistic tastes, but his mother secretly helped him study art. He was apprenticed to a china dealer, then worked as a china painter in the Staffordshire Potteries, then went to London. In his early years he painted classical figures with landscapes, such as Hylas and the Nymphs, and later he moved to genre subjects and rustic groups. Around 1813 he tried portraits, small full-lengths with landscape backgrounds. He died in 1847.

David Loggan was baptised in Danzig to English and Scottish parents. He studied under Willem Hondius there and under Crispijn van de Passe II in Amsterdam, then moved to London in the late 1650s. His work included the title page of the folio Book of Common Prayer and miniature portraits as plumbago drawings. He left London for Nuffield in 1665 to avoid the Great Plague. As public sculptor to Oxford University he drew and engraved all the Oxford colleges in bird's-eye views, published as Oxonia illustrata in 1675. He died in 1692.

At eighteen H. Lyman Saÿen designed a large induction coil that was cited at the World's Columbian Exposition. In 1897 he received a patent for a self-regulating x-ray tube, the first of its kind to solve the problem of unstable output when the gas pressure dropped. During the Spanish-American War he ran the medical x-ray laboratory at Fort McPherson, Georgia, until typhoid fever got him discharged. Back in Philadelphia he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and studied under Thomas Anshutz. He also became an abstract artist.
